claim: A small-molecule communication mechanism was discovered in a range of Bacillus-infecting bacteriophages.
source: Recently, a small-molecule communication mechanism was discovered in a range of Bacillus-infecting bacteriophages, which these temperate phages use to inform their lysis-lysogeny decision.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Erez et al., 2017) mentioned later in the manuscript.

claim: Temperate phages use the small-molecule communication mechanism to inform their lysis-lysogeny decision.
source: Recently, a small-molecule communication mechanism was discovered in a range of Bacillus-infecting bacteriophages, which these temperate phages use to inform their lysis-lysogeny decision.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Erez et al., 2017).

claim: A communication strategy in which phages use the lytic cycle early in an outbreak but switch to the lysogenic cycle later is favoured over a bet-hedging strategy.
source: We present a mathematical model of the ecological and evolutionary dynamics of such viral communication and show that a communication strategy in which phages use the lytic cycle early in an outbreak (when susceptible host cells are abundant) but switch to the lysogenic cycle later (when susceptible cells become scarce) is favoured over a bet-hedging strategy in which cells are lysogenised with constant probability.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mathematical modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Phage communication can evolve only if phage-bacteria populations are regularly perturbed away from their equilibrium state.
source: However, such phage communication can evolve only if phage-bacteria populations are regularly perturbed away from their equilibrium state, so that acute outbreaks of phage infections in pools of susceptible cells continue to occur.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mathematical modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Communication between individuals is common among microbes.
source: For several decades now, it has been recognised that communication between individuals is not limited to multicellular organisms, but is also common among microbes.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations.

claim: Bacterial quorum sensing is a process in which bacteria secrete signalling molecules to infer the local cell density and consequently coordinate the expression of certain genes.
source: The best-known example of microbial communication is bacterial quorum sensing, a process in which bacteria secrete signalling molecules to infer the local cell density and consequently coordinate the expression of certain genes (Nealson et al., 1970; Miller and Bassler, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Bioluminescence is under quorum-sensing control.
source: A wide variety of bacterial behaviours have been found to be under quorum-sensing control (Miller and Bassler, 2001; Hense and Schuster, 2015), including bioluminescence (Nealson et al., 1970), virulence (Antunes et al., 2010), cooperative public good production (Diggle et al., 2007; Darch et al., 2012), and antimicrobial toxin production (Cornforth and Foster, 2013; Kleerebezem and Quadri, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Virulence is under quorum-sensing control.
source: A wide variety of bacterial behaviours have been found to be under quorum-sensing control (Miller and Bassler, 2001; Hense and Schuster, 2015), including bioluminescence (Nealson et al., 1970), virulence (Antunes et al., 2010), cooperative public good production (Diggle et al., 2007; Darch et al., 2012), and antimicrobial toxin production (Cornforth and Foster, 2013; Kleerebezem and Quadri, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cooperative public good production is under quorum-sensing control.
source: A wide variety of bacterial behaviours have been found to be under quorum-sensing control (Miller and Bassler, 2001; Hense and Schuster, 2015), including bioluminescence (Nealson et al., 1970), virulence (Antunes et al., 2010), cooperative public good production (Diggle et al., 2007; Darch et al., 2012), and antimicrobial toxin production (Cornforth and Foster, 2013; Kleerebezem and Quadri, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Antimicrobial toxin production is under quorum-sensing control.
source: A wide variety of bacterial behaviours have been found to be under quorum-sensing control (Miller and Bassler, 2001; Hense and Schuster, 2015), including bioluminescence (Nealson et al., 1970), virulence (Antunes et al., 2010), cooperative public good production (Diggle et al., 2007; Darch et al., 2012), and antimicrobial toxin production (Cornforth and Foster, 2013; Kleerebezem and Quadri, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Some bacterial viruses use signalling molecules to communicate.
source: Remarkably, it has recently been discovered that even some bacterial viruses (bacteriophages or phages for short) use signalling molecules to communicate (Erez et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Bacteriophages of the SPbeta group encode a small signalling peptide named 'arbitrium'.
source: Bacteriophages of the SPbeta group, a genus in the order of Caudovirales of viruses that infect Bacillus bacteria, encode a small signalling peptide, named 'arbitrium', which is secreted when the phages infect bacteria (Erez et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Arbitrium is secreted when the phages infect bacteria.
source: Bacteriophages of the SPbeta group, a genus in the order of Caudovirales of viruses that infect Bacillus bacteria, encode a small signalling peptide, named 'arbitrium', which is secreted when the phages infect bacteria (Erez et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: SPbeta group phages are temperate viruses.
source: These phages are temperate viruses, meaning that each time a phage infects a bacterium, it makes a life-cycle decision: to enter either (i) the lytic cycle, inducing an active infection in which tens to thousands of new phage particles are produced and released through host-cell lysis, or (ii) the lysogenic cycle, inducing a latent infection in which the phage DNA is integrated in the host cell's genome (or episomally maintained) and the phage remains dormant until it is reactivated.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Temperate phages make a life-cycle decision between the lytic cycle and the lysogenic cycle each time they infect a bacterium.
source: These phages are temperate viruses, meaning that each time a phage infects a bacterium, it makes a life-cycle decision: to enter either (i) the lytic cycle, inducing an active infection in which tens to thousands of new phage particles are produced and released through host-cell lysis, or (ii) the lysogenic cycle, inducing a latent infection in which the phage DNA is integrated in the host cell's genome (or episomally maintained) and the phage remains dormant until it is reactivated.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: The lytic cycle induces an active infection in which tens to thousands of new phage particles are produced and released through host-cell lysis.
source: These phages are temperate viruses, meaning that each time a phage infects a bacterium, it makes a life-cycle decision: to enter either (i) the lytic cycle, inducing an active infection in which tens to thousands of new phage particles are produced and released through host-cell lysis, or (ii) the lysogenic cycle, inducing a latent infection in which the phage DNA is integrated in the host cell's genome (or episomally maintained) and the phage remains dormant until it is reactivated.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: The lysogenic cycle induces a latent infection in which the phage DNA is integrated in the host cell's genome and the phage remains dormant until it is reactivated.
source: These phages are temperate viruses, meaning that each time a phage infects a bacterium, it makes a life-cycle decision: to enter either (i) the lytic cycle, inducing an active infection in which tens to thousands of new phage particles are produced and released through host-cell lysis, or (ii) the lysogenic cycle, inducing a latent infection in which the phage DNA is integrated in the host cell's genome (or episomally maintained) and the phage remains dormant until it is reactivated.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: The lysis-lysogeny decision is informed by the arbitrium produced in nearby previous infections.
source: This lysis-lysogeny decision is informed by the arbitrium produced in nearby previous infections: extracellular arbitrium is taken up by cells and inhibits the phage's lysogeny-inhibition factors, thus increasing the propenstiy towards lysogeny of subsequent infections (Erez et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Extracellular arbitrium is taken up by cells and inhibits the phage's lysogeny-inhibition factors, thus increasing the propensity towards lysogeny of subsequent infections.
source: This lysis-lysogeny decision is informed by the arbitrium produced in nearby previous infections: extracellular arbitrium is taken up by cells and inhibits the phage's lysogeny-inhibition factors, thus increasing the propenstiy towards lysogeny of subsequent infections (Erez et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Peptide communication is used to promote lysogeny when many infections have occurred.
source: Hence, peptide communication is used to promote lysogeny when many infections have occurred.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the mechanism described in the cited work.

claim: Similar arbitrium-like systems have been found in a range of different phages.
source: Similar arbitrium-like systems have now been found in a range of different phages (Stokar-Avihail et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Phages with arbitrium-like systems each use a slightly different signalling peptide and do not seem to respond to the signals of other phages.
source: Notably, these phages each use a slightly different signalling peptide and do not seem to respond to the signals of other phages (Erez et al., 2017; Stokar-Avihail et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Lysogeny can evolve as a survival mechanism for phages to overcome periods in which the density of susceptible cells is too low to sustain a lytic infection.
source: Early modelling work found that lysogeny can evolve as a survival mechanism for phages to overcome periods in which the density of susceptible cells is too low to sustain a lytic infection (Stewart and Levin, 1984; Maslov and Sneppen, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: Selection pressures on phage virulence change over the course of an epidemic, favouring a virulent phage strain early on but a less virulent phage strain later in the epidemic.
source: In line with these model predictions, a combination of modelling and experimental work showed that selection pressures on phage virulence change over the course of an epidemic, favouring a virulent phage strain early on, when the density of susceptible cells is high, but a less virulent (i.e. lysogenic) phage strain later in the epidemic, when susceptible cells have become scarce (Berngruber et al., 2013; Gandon, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior modeling and experimental work.

claim: If phages, lysogenised cells, and susceptible cells coexist for long periods of time, less and less virulent phages are selected.
source: Other modelling work has shown that if phages, lysogenised cells, and susceptible cells coexist for long periods of time, less and less virulent phages are selected (Mittler, 1996; Wahl et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: Phage exploitation leads to a low susceptible cell density, and hence a virulent strategy no longer pays off because few cells are available to infect.
source: This happens because phage exploitation leads to a low susceptible cell density, and hence a virulent strategy in which phages rapidly lyse their host cell to release new phage particles that can then infect other cells no longer pays off (because few cells are available to infect).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the modeling results cited.

claim: The arbitrium system may have evolved to allow phages to cope with the changing environment during an epidemic.
source: Erez et al., 2017 propose that the arbitrium system may have evolved to allow phages to cope with the changing environment during an epidemic, allowing the phages to exploit available susceptible bacteria through the lytic cycle when few infections have so far taken place and hence the concentration of arbitrium is low, while entering the lysogenic cycle when many infections have taken place and the arbitrium concentration has hence increased.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis proposed by cited authors.

claim: In T-even phages, both the length of the latent period of an infection and the subsequent burst size increase if additional phages adsorb to the cell while it is infected.
source: In the obligately lytic T-even phages, both the length of the latent period of an infection and the subsequent burst size increase if additional phages adsorb to the cell while it is infected – a process called lysis inhibition (Hershey, 1946; Doermann, 1948; Abedon, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In temperate phage λ, the propensity towards lysogeny increases with the number of co-infecting virions.
source: In the temperate phage λ, the propensity towards lysogeny increases with the number of co-infecting virions, called the multiplicity of infection (MOI) (Kourilsky, 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The effect of the number of phage adsorptions on an infection can be selected as a phage adaptation to host-cell density.
source: In both cases, modelling work has shown that the effect of the number of phage adsorptions on an infection can be selected as a phage adaptation to host-cell density, as it allows phages to switch from a virulent infection strategy (i.e. a short latent period or a low lysogeny propensity) when the phage:host-cell ratio is low to a less virulent strategy (i.e. a longer latent period or higher lysogeny propensity) when the phage:host-cell ratio is high (Abedon, 1989; Abedon, 1990; Sinha et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: Arbitrium communication can evolve.
source: We show that arbitrium communication can indeed evolve and that communicating phages consistently outcompete phages with non-communicating bet-hedging strategies.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mathematical modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Communicating phages consistently outcompete phages with non-communicating bet-hedging strategies.
source: We show that arbitrium communication can indeed evolve and that communicating phages consistently outcompete phages with non-communicating bet-hedging strategies.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mathematical modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Communication evolves only if the phages regularly cause new outbreaks in substantial pools of susceptible host cells.
source: We however find that communication evolves under certain conditions only, namely if the phages regularly cause new outbreaks in substantial pools of susceptible host cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mathematical modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: When communication evolves, a communication strategy is selected in which phages use arbitrium to switch from a fully lytic to a fully lysogenic strategy when approximately half of all susceptible cells have been infected.
source: Moreover, when communication evolves under such conditions, we predict that a communication strategy is selected in which phages use arbitrium to switch from a fully lytic to a fully lysogenic strategy when approximately half of all susceptible cells have been infected.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mathematical modeling results and analytical derivations presented in the manuscript.

claim: The results are remarkably robust against variation in the density of bacteria.
source: Finally, we investigate how reliable the arbitrium signal needs to be for such communication to evolve, and show that the results are remarkably robust against variation in the density of bacteria.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mathematical modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The model uses ordinary differential equations to describe a well-mixed system consisting of susceptible bacteria, lysogens, and free phages.
source: Following earlier models (e.g. Stewart and Levin, 1984; Berngruber et al., 2013; Sinha et al., 2017; Wahl et al., 2018), we use ordinary differential equations to describe a well-mixed system consisting of susceptible bacteria, lysogens (i.e. lysogenically infected bacteria), and free phages, but extend this system to include an arbitrium-like signalling peptide (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim describes the modeling approach used in the manuscript.

claim: The model extends earlier models to include an arbitrium-like signalling peptide.
source: Following earlier models (e.g. Stewart and Levin, 1984; Berngruber et al., 2013; Sinha et al., 2017; Wahl et al., 2018), we use ordinary differential equations to describe a well-mixed system consisting of susceptible bacteria, lysogens (i.e. lysogenically infected bacteria), and free phages, but extend this system to include an arbitrium-like signalling peptide (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim describes the modeling approach used in the manuscript.

claim: Phages do not affect the growth of lysogenised host cells in the model.
source: For simplicity, we consider phages that do not affect the growth of lysogenised host cells; susceptible bacteria and lysogens hence both grow logistically with the same growth rate r and carrying capacity K.
evidence: This claim describes a simplifying assumption in the model.

claim: Susceptible bacteria and lysogens both grow logistically with the same growth rate r and carrying capacity K.
source: For simplicity, we consider phages that do not affect the growth of lysogenised host cells; susceptible bacteria and lysogens hence both grow logistically with the same growth rate r and carrying capacity K.
evidence: This claim describes a model assumption.

claim: Lysogens are spontaneously induced at a low rate α.
source: Lysogens are spontaneously induced at a low rate α, after which they lyse and release a burst of B free phages per lysing cell.
evidence: This claim describes a model parameter.

claim: Free phage particles decay at a rate δ.
source: Free phage particles decay at a rate δ and adsorb to bacteria at a rate a.
evidence: This claim describes a model parameter.

claim: Free phage particles adsorb to bacteria at a rate a.
source: Free phage particles decay at a rate δ and adsorb to bacteria at a rate a.
evidence: This claim describes a model parameter.

claim: Adsorptions to lysogens result in the decay of the infecting phage, describing the effect of superinfection immunity.
source: Adsorptions to lysogens result in the decay of the infecting phage, thus describing the well-known effect of superinfection immunity (Hutchison and Sinsheimer, 1971; Susskind et al., 1974; McAllister and Barrett, 1977; Kliem and Dreiseikelmann, 1989; Bondy-Denomy et al., 2016), whereas adsorptions to susceptible bacteria result in infections with success probability b.
evidence: This claim describes a model feature supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Adsorptions to susceptible bacteria result in infections with success probability b.
source: Adsorptions to lysogens result in the decay of the infecting phage, thus describing the well-known effect of superinfection immunity (Hutchison and Sinsheimer, 1971; Susskind et al., 1974; McAllister and Barrett, 1977; Kliem and Dreiseikelmann, 1989; Bondy-Denomy et al., 2016), whereas adsorptions to susceptible bacteria result in infections with success probability b.
evidence: This claim describes a model parameter.

claim: The lytic cycle is fast compared to both bacterial growth and the lysogenic cycle.
source: We consider the lytic cycle to be fast compared to both bacterial growth and the lysogenic cycle (Stewart and Levin, 1984; Berngruber et al., 2013; Sinha et al., 2017; Wahl et al., 2018), so that a lytic infection can be modelled as immediate lysis releasing a burst of B free phages.
evidence: This claim describes a model assumption supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A lytic infection can be modelled as immediate lysis releasing a burst of B free phages.
source: We consider the lytic cycle to be fast compared to both bacterial growth and the lysogenic cycle (Stewart and Levin, 1984; Berngruber et al., 2013; Sinha et al., 2017; Wahl et al., 2018), so that a lytic infection can be modelled as immediate lysis releasing a burst of B free phages.
evidence: This claim describes a model assumption.

claim: The genes encoding arbitrium production are among the first genes to be expressed when a phage infects a host cell.
source: Since the genes encoding arbitrium production are among the first genes to be expressed when a phage infects a host cell (Erez et al., 2017; Stokar-Avihail et al., 2019), each infection leads to an immediate increase of the arbitrium concentration A by an increment c.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Each infection leads to an immediate increase of the arbitrium concentration A by an increment c.
source: Since the genes encoding arbitrium production are among the first genes to be expressed when a phage infects a host cell (Erez et al., 2017; Stokar-Avihail et al., 2019), each infection leads to an immediate increase of the arbitrium concentration A by an increment c.
evidence: This claim describes a model feature.

claim: Arbitrium does not decay spontaneously in the model.
source: Arbitrium does not decay spontaneously in the model (since it is a small peptide, spontaneous extracellular degradation is considered to be negligible), but it is taken up by bacteria at a rate u (e.g. through general bacterial peptide importers such as OPP [Erez et al., 2017]), and then degraded intracellularly, thus reducing the arbitrium concentration A.
evidence: This claim describes a model assumption.

claim: Arbitrium is taken up by bacteria at a rate u and then degraded intracellularly.
source: Arbitrium does not decay spontaneously in the model (since it is a small peptide, spontaneous extracellular degradation is considered to be negligible), but it is taken up by bacteria at a rate u (e.g. through general bacterial peptide importers such as OPP [Erez et al., 2017]), and then degraded intracellularly, thus reducing the arbitrium concentration A.
evidence: This claim describes a model feature supported by citation.

claim: Considering the equilibrium states is insufficient to understand the evolution of arbitrium communication.
source: However, we will here argue that to understand the evolution of arbitrium communication, and the lysis-lysogeny decision in general, considering the equilibrium states is insufficient.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the modeling analysis.

claim: When the system approaches an equilibrium state, the densities of susceptible cells and phages become constant, and so does the arbitrium concentration.
source: But when the system approaches an equilibrium state, the densities of susceptible cells and phages become constant, and so does the arbitrium concentration.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the model structure.

claim: Equilibrium conditions defeat the purpose of small-molecule communication such as the arbitrium system.
source: Equilibrium conditions hence defeat the purpose of small-molecule communication such as the arbitrium system.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the modeling analysis.

claim: Evolution of small-molecule communication must be driven by dynamical ecological processes.
source: Evolution of small-molecule communication must be driven by dynamical ecological processes, and hence can only be studied in populations that are regularly perturbed away from their ecological steady state.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the modeling analysis.

claim: Under equilibrium conditions natural selection can act on the lysis-lysogeny decision only if infections still take place.
source: Secondly, under equilibrium conditions natural selection can act on the lysis-lysogeny decision only if infections still take place, and hence lysis-lysogeny decisions are still taken.
evidence: This claim is an inference from evolutionary principles.

claim: If the phage population is viable, the model converges to one of two qualitatively different equilibria.
source: If the phage population is viable (i.e. if the parameter values are such that the phages proliferate when introduced into a fully susceptible host population), the model converges to one of two qualitatively different equilibria, depending on parameter conditions (Appendix A2): either (i) susceptible host cells, lysogens and free phages all coexist, or (ii) all susceptible host cells have been infected so that only lysogens and free phages remain.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mathematical analysis in the manuscript.

claim: Only a narrow sliver of parameter conditions permits a stable equilibrium of type (i).
source: However, only a narrow sliver of parameter conditions permits a stable equilibrium of type (i) (Sinha et al., 2017; Cortes et al., 2019), and when we estimated reasonable parameter conditions based on a variety of well-studied phages, we found that they typically lead to a stable equilibrium of type (ii) (Appendix A2, parameter estimates based on Little et al., 1999; De Paepe and Taddei, 2006; Wang, 2006; Shao and Wang, 2008; Zong et al., 2010; Berngruber et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and the analysis in the manuscript.

claim: Reasonable parameter conditions typically lead to a stable equilibrium of type (ii).
source: However, only a narrow sliver of parameter conditions permits a stable equilibrium of type (i) (Sinha et al., 2017; Cortes et al., 2019), and when we estimated reasonable parameter conditions based on a variety of well-studied phages, we found that they typically lead to a stable equilibrium of type (ii) (Appendix A2, parameter estimates based on Little et al., 1999; De Paepe and Taddei, 2006; Wang, 2006; Shao and Wang, 2008; Zong et al., 2010; Berngruber et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis in the manuscript and citations to prior work.

claim: Phage infections tend to be highly effective due to their large burst size and consequent high infectivity.
source: This is because phage infections tend to be highly effective: their large burst size and consequent high infectivity cause temperate phages to completely deplete susceptible host cell populations, replacing them with lysogens that are immune to superinfection and hence have a strong competitive advantage over the susceptible cells (Bossi et al., 2003; Gama et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Temperate phages completely deplete susceptible host cell populations, replacing them with lysogens that are immune to superinfection.
source: This is because phage infections tend to be highly effective: their large burst size and consequent high infectivity cause temperate phages to completely deplete susceptible host cell populations, replacing them with lysogens that are immune to superinfection and hence have a strong competitive advantage over the susceptible cells (Bossi et al., 2003; Gama et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Lysogens have a strong competitive advantage over susceptible cells.
source: This is because phage infections tend to be highly effective: their large burst size and consequent high infectivity cause temperate phages to completely deplete susceptible host cell populations, replacing them with lysogens that are immune to superinfection and hence have a strong competitive advantage over the susceptible cells (Bossi et al., 2003; Gama et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Under common parameter conditions, after a short epidemic the susceptible cells population is depleted and no more infections take place.
source: Under common parameter conditions, after a short epidemic the susceptible cells population is hence depleted and no more infections take place, causing the competition between different phage variants to cease (see Figure 2A for example dynamics).
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Once the susceptible cell population has collapsed, free phages no longer cause new infections and are hence 'dead ends'.
source: This result can be explained by considering the dynamics within a passaging episode (see Figure 2A): Once the susceptible cell population has collapsed, free phages no longer cause new infections and are hence 'dead ends'.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: When the time between passages is sufficiently long, the phage type that is most frequent in the sample that is eventually passaged is the one that is most frequent in the population of lysogens.
source: Hence, when the time between passages is sufficiently long, the phage type that is most frequent in the sample that is eventually passaged is the one that is most frequent in the population of lysogens (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: A population consisting of a dominant variant and its close mutants is called a quasi-species.
source: Such a population consisting of a dominant variant and its close mutants is called a quasi-species (Eigen, 1971).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: If the passaged sample consists of the full system, almost identical results are obtained.
source: If instead the passaged sample consists of the full system (susceptible cells, lysogens, and phages), almost identical results are obtained (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The contribution of passaged lysogens to the new outbreak does not alter the relative frequency of phage variants.
source: Since lysogens need to be induced to contribute to a new outbreak and the induction rate α is the same for all phage variants, the contribution of passaged lysogens to the new outbreak does not alter the relative frequency of phage variants.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the model structure.

claim: These phages employ a bet-hedging strategy by investing a small part of their infection events in the production of lysogens.
source: These phages employ a bet-hedging strategy: throughout the epidemic they 'invest' a small part of their infection events in the production of lysogens, such that they are maximally represented in the eventual lysogen population.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: If the phage density is low at the start of a passaging episode or if the phages have a small effective burst size, it takes a while before the phage population has grown sufficiently to cause the susceptible population to collapse.
source: If the phage density is low at the start of a passaging episode or if the phages have a small effective burst size, it takes a while before the phage population has grown sufficiently to cause the susceptible population to collapse.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the model dynamics.

claim: The arbitrium concentration increases over the course of the epidemic.
source: The arbitrium concentration increases over the course of the epidemic, and the phage variants switch from lytic infection to lysogen production at different times because of their different response thresholds.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The arbitrium concentration during the early epidemic is a direct reflection of the fraction of susceptible cells that have so far been infected.
source: The arbitrium concentration during the early epidemic then is a direct reflection of the fraction of susceptible cells that have so far been infected.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the model structure.

claim: The communicating phage quickly invades a population of bet-hedging phages and takes over.
source: The communicating phage quickly invades on a population of bet-hedging phages and takes over, confirming that communication is indeed favoured over bet-hedging.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Communication is favoured over bet-hedging.
source: The communicating phage quickly invades on a population of bet-hedging phages and takes over, confirming that communication is indeed favoured over bet-hedging.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The passaged arbitrium does not significantly affect the outbreak dynamics.
source: The passaged arbitrium does not significantly affect the outbreak dynamics either, because its concentration after dilution is much lower than the response threshold θ of the phage variants that are selected.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: The analytical approximation provides a good prediction for the response threshold value that is selected over evolutionary time, especially for phages with high effective burst size.
source: We see that Equation 6 provides a good prediction for the response threshold value that is selected over evolutionary time, especially for phages with high effective burst size (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of analytical and simulation results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For phages with a very small effective burst size, the response threshold selected in the simulations tends to be lower than the analytical approximation.
source: For phages with a very small effective burst size, the response threshold selected in the simulations tends to be lower than the analytical approximation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The evolutionarily stable response threshold causes phages to switch infection strategy somewhere in the middle of the epidemic.
source: It makes sense that the evolutionarily stable response threshold causes phages to switch infection strategy somewhere in the middle of the epidemic: if a phage variant switches to the lysogenic strategy too early, its free phage population does not expand enough to compete with phages that switch later, but if it switches too late, the susceptible-cell density has decreased to such a degree that the phage has missed the window of opportunity for lysogen production.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: For phages with a high effective burst size, the balance between fast production of phage progeny and eventual production of sufficient lysogens occurs around the time that half of the available susceptible cells have been infected.
source: For phages with a high effective burst size, this balance occurs around the time that half of the available susceptible cells have been infected.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the analytical results.

claim: Phages with lower effective burst size are predicted to switch later because these phages need to invest a larger portion of the available susceptible cells in the production of free phages.
source: Phages with lower effective burst size are, however, predicted to switch later, because these phages need to invest a larger portion of the available susceptible cells in the production of free phages to produce a sufficient pool of phages that can later form lysogens.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the analytical results.

claim: For natural phages in general, if they evolve an arbitrium-like communication system, communication will be used to switch from causing mostly lytic to mostly lysogenic infections when in an outbreak approximately half of the pool of susceptible bacteria has been infected.
source: Hence, for natural phages in general, we predict that if they evolve an arbitrium-like communication system, communication will be used to switch from causing mostly lytic to mostly lysogenic infections when in an outbreak approximately half of the pool of susceptible bacteria has been infected.
evidence: This claim is a prediction based on the modeling results.

claim: Even if the carrying capacity varies with a standard deviation up to one third of its mean value, the communication strategy is still selected.
source: In other words, even if the carrying capacity varies with a standard deviation up to one third of its mean value, the communication strategy described in the previous section is still selected.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results.

claim: If the carrying capacity strongly varies between passaging episodes, phages with a response threshold value larger than the bacterial carrying capacity do not produce any lysogens during such an outbreak, which is disastrous for their long-term fitness.
source: These results make sense: if the carrying capacity strongly varies between passaging episodes, the phages regularly cause outbreaks in bacterial populations with low density. Phages with a response threshold value larger than the bacterial carrying capacity do not produce any lysogens during such an outbreak, which is disastrous for their long-term fitness.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: Lower response thresholds are selected when carrying capacity varies strongly.
source: Hence, lower response thresholds are selected.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: In highly variable conditions, phages are selected to switch from a lytic strategy very early in the epidemic to a bet-hedging strategy later.
source: In highly variable conditions, phages are hence selected to switch from a lytic strategy very early in the epidemic to a bet-hedging strategy later.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: Even under very high variation of bacterial density a form of arbitrium communication is still favoured over completely bet-hedging strategies.
source: Hence, even under very high variation of bacterial density a form of arbitrium communication (in which phages use the arbitrium signal to switch from a lytic to a bet-hedging strategy) is still favoured over completely bet-hedging strategies.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results.

claim: The serial-passaging set-up of the model is crucial for the evolution of the lysis-lysogeny decision and arbitrium communication.
source: The serial-passaging set-up of the model is crucial for the evolution of the lysis-lysogeny decision and arbitrium communication.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the modeling analysis.

claim: The serial-passaging set-up ensures that the phages are regularly exposed to susceptible cells, thus maintaining selection pressure on the lysis-lysogeny decision.
source: Firstly, it ensures that the phages are regularly exposed to susceptible cells, thus maintaining selection pressure on the lysis-lysogeny decision.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the modeling analysis.

claim: Most temperate phage outbreaks will completely deplete pools of susceptible bacteria, resulting in a bacterial population consisting of lysogens only in which the phage no longer replicates through infection.
source: Because of their high infectivity (see Materials and methods section and De Paepe and Taddei, 2006; Wang, 2006), most temperate phage outbreaks will completely deplete pools of susceptible bacteria, resulting in a bacterial population consisting of lysogens only in which the phage no longer replicates through infection (Bossi et al., 2003; Gama et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The bet-hedging strategy found in the absence of phage communication is a mechanism to deal with periods of low susceptible cell availability.
source: The bet-hedging strategy we found in the absence of phage communication is a mechanism to deal with these (self-inflicted) periods of low susceptible cell availability, consistent with earlier studies (Maslov and Sneppen, 2015; Sinha et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is an inference from the modeling results and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The serial-passaging set-up imposes a dynamic of repeated epidemics in which a small number of phages is introduced into a relatively large pool of susceptible cells.
source: Secondly, the serial-passaging set-up imposes a dynamic of repeated epidemics in which a small number of phages is introduced into a relatively large pool of susceptible cells.
evidence: This claim describes the modeling approach.

claim: The arbitrium concentration provides a reliable cue for a phage's lysis-lysogeny decision only if it is low at the beginning of an epidemic and subsequently builds up to reflect the fraction of cells that have so far been infected.
source: Such dynamics are necessary for the arbitrium system to function: the arbitrium concentration provides a reliable cue for a phage's lysis-lysogeny decision only if it is low at the beginning of an epidemic and subsequently builds up to reflect the fraction of cells that have so far been infected.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the modeling analysis.

claim: Spatial structure can ensure a regular exposure to susceptible cells by maintaining a global susceptible population even though susceptible bacteria may be depleted in local environments.
source: One major factor that can ensure a regular exposure to susceptible cells (the first requirement) is spatial structure. If phages mostly infect bacteria that are physically close to them, a global susceptible population can be maintained even though susceptible bacteria may be depleted in local environments (Kerr et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is speculation supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Spatial structure has been shown to greatly influence phage evolution, for instance by promoting the selection of less virulent strains.
source: Indeed, spatial structure has been shown to greatly influence phage evolution, for instance by promoting the selection of less virulent strains that deplete their local host populations more slowly (Kerr et al., 2006; Heilmann et al., 2010; Berngruber et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: For small-molecule communication to evolve, the phages would have to undergo repeated, possibly localised, outbreak dynamics.
source: For small-molecule communication to evolve, however, the phages would also have to undergo repeated, possibly localised, outbreak dynamics (the second requirement).
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the modeling results.

claim: Phages might encounter large pools of newly susceptible bacteria if they escape superinfection immunity through mutation.
source: Alternatively, phages might encounter large pools of newly susceptible bacteria if they escape superinfection immunity through mutation (Zinder, 1958; Bailone and Devoret, 1978; Scott et al., 1978).
evidence: This claim is speculation supported by citations to prior work.

claim: If the escape mutation occurs after the arbitrium produced during previous epidemics has been degraded, the newly produced arbitrium functions as a reliable signal of susceptible cell density for the new phage variant.
source: If the escape mutation occurs after the arbitrium produced during previous epidemics has been degraded, this problem does not occur and the newly produced arbitrium does function as a reliable signal of susceptible cell density for the new phage variant.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the modeling analysis.

claim: If the escape mutation occurs while the arbitrium concentration is still high from previous outbreaks, the new phage variant will cause lysogenic infections while in fact the lytic cycle should be favoured.
source: If, however, the escape mutation occurs while the arbitrium concentration is still high from previous outbreaks, the new phage variant will cause lysogenic infections while in fact the lytic cycle should be favoured.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the modeling analysis.

claim: There will be selection pressure on the new phage variant to acquire additional mutations that change its signal specificity.
source: There will then be selection pressure on the new phage variant to acquire additional mutations that change its signal specificity.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on evolutionary reasoning.

claim: Selection pressure to change signal specificity might in part explain the large diversity of phage signalling peptides observed.
source: This might in part explain the large diversity of phage signalling peptides observed (Erez et al., 2017; Stokar-Avihail et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is speculation supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Under repeated epidemics, selection on the lysis-lysogeny decision and arbitrium signalling is limited to the relatively short window of time in which all present susceptible cells become infected.
source: Above we have argued, however, that under repeated epidemics, such as caused by serial passaging, selection on the lysis-lysogeny decision and arbitrium signalling is limited to the relatively short window of time in which all (locally) present susceptible cells become infected: afterwards no new infections occur and arbitrium therefore has no effect.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the modeling analysis.

claim: During the short time window of an epidemic, the density of lysogens is still low, and any arbitrium produced by lysogens contributes little to the information already conveyed by arbitrium produced during infection events.
source: During this short time window, the density of lysogens is still low, and any arbitrium produced by lysogens contributes little to the information already conveyed by arbitrium produced during infection events.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the modeling analysis.

claim: Under repeated epidemics that completely deplete pools of susceptible cells, the effects of arbitrium production by lysogens are likely very minimal.
source: Hence, our model predicts that, under repeated epidemics that completely deplete (local) pools of susceptible cells, the effects of arbitrium production by lysogens are likely very minimal.
evidence: This claim is a prediction based on the modeling analysis.

claim: Arbitrium production by lysogens can be effective only if lysogens and susceptible cells coexist over sufficiently long periods of time.
source: Arbitrium production by lysogens can be effective only if lysogens and susceptible cells coexist over sufficiently long periods of time, such that infection events occur in the presence of lysogens.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the modeling analysis.

claim: In the model, coexistence between lysogens and susceptible cells is highly unlikely.
source: In the model, we found that such coexistence is highly unlikely.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results.

claim: Coexistence between lysogens and susceptible cells might happen through a constant inflow of susceptible cells because of cell migration, or through the loss of superinfection immunity by lysogens.
source: Coexistence between lysogens and susceptible cells might, however, happen under circumstances that were not included in our model, for instance through a constant inflow of susceptible cells because of cell migration, or through the loss of superinfection immunity by lysogens.
evidence: This claim is speculation about factors not included in the model.

claim: The model predicts that phages using small-molecule communication would be selected to switch from a lytic to a lysogenic strategy once approximately half of the available susceptible bacteria have been lytically infected.
source: Intriguingly, our model predicts that phages using small-molecule communication to coordinate their lysis-lysogeny decision would be selected to switch from a lytic to a lysogenic strategy once approximately half of the available susceptible bacteria have been lytically infected.
evidence: This claim is a prediction based on the modeling results.

claim: For the arbitrium signal to carry reliable information about the density of remaining susceptible cells, the initial concentration of susceptible bacteria has to be similar from outbreak to outbreak.
source: For the arbitrium signal to carry reliable information about the density of remaining susceptible cells, the initial concentration of susceptible bacteria has to be similar from outbreak to outbreak.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the model structure.

claim: Arbitrium-like communication can evolve even if the bacterial carrying capacity is highly variable.
source: Surprisingly, this turned out not to be the case. We found that arbitrium-like communication could evolve even if the bacterial carrying capacity was highly variable.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results.

claim: In highly variable environments, phages are predicted to start their lysogen production earlier in an outbreak and then do so in a bet-hedging way.
source: In highly variable environments, we predict the selection of phages that start their lysogen production earlier in an outbreak (i.e. phages that have a low response threshold), and then do so in a bet-hedging way (i.e. with a lysogeny propensity much smaller than 1).
evidence: This claim is a prediction based on the modeling results.

claim: Few details are known about the response curve of phages' lysogeny propensity to the arbitrium concentration.
source: In fact, few details are known so far about the response curve of phages' lysogeny propensity to the arbitrium concentration.
evidence: This claim is based on the current state of knowledge.

claim: In the model, the response to arbitrium was implemented as a stepwise function.
source: In the model, we chose to implement the response to arbitrium as a stepwise function.
evidence: This claim describes the modeling approach.

claim: Phages will use the arbitrium signal to adjust their infection strategy to whichever strategy currently yields most progeny phage on the long run, regardless of the precise shape of the response curve.
source: While this would alter some of our results (e.g. pinpointing an arbitrium concentration at which the phages switch infection strategy becomes harder, if not impossible), we do not expect the results in general to depend on the precise shape of the response curve: phages will still use the arbitrium signal to adjust their infection strategy to whichever strategy currently yields most progeny phage on the long run.
evidence: This claim is speculation about the robustness of the results.

claim: The Vibrio cholerae-infecting phage VP882 'eavesdrops' on a quorum-sensing signal produced by its host bacteria, favouring lytic over lysogenic infections when the host density is high.
source: For instance, the Vibrio cholerae-infecting phage VP882 'eavesdrops' on a quorum-sensing signal produced by its host bacteria, favouring lytic over lysogenic infections when the host density is high (Silpe and Bassler, 2019),
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In coliphages λ and T4 and several phages infecting Enterococcus faecalis, the induction of prophages is affected by bacterial quorum sensing signals.
source: while in coliphages λ and T4 and several phages infecting Enterococcus faecalis, the induction of prophages, that is, the lysogeny-lysis decision, is affected by bacterial quorum sensing signals (Ghosh et al., 2009; Rossmann et al., 2015; Laganenka et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mathematical and computational modelling can help to better understand the ecology and evolution of phage regulation mechanisms.
source: Mathematical and computational modelling can thus help to better understand the ecology and evolution of these fascinating regulation mechanisms as well.
evidence: This claim is speculation about the utility of modeling approaches.
